tasks.title: Selectable model and effort per harness
criteria: Add one module under src/ that answers which models and which efforts per model each harness offers; harness.ts, claude-adapter.ts and codex-adapter.ts use it instead of their own hard-coded model and effort checks.

Claude offers a static catalog of exact model IDs claude-opus-5-5, claude-sonnet-5-5, claude-haiku-5-5 and claude-fable-5-2, each with efforts low, medium, high, xhigh and max (the values accepted by `claude --effort`).

Codex offers the models returned by the app-server RPC model/list (all pages, following nextCursor, hidden models excluded) and, per model, the efforts listed in its supportedReasoningEfforts[].reasoningEffort.

The Claude-only restriction 'Claude requires Opus 5.5 medium' and the ClaudeAdapter constructor check 'Unsupported Claude model or effort' are removed; any model and effort combination present in the Claude catalog is accepted and passed to `claude --model <id> --effort <level>`, and the existing pinned-model verification of the init, assistant and result messages stays in force for the selected model.

A model or effort that the selected harness does not offer, or an effort the selected model does not support, is refused before allocation with exit code 4 and a diagnostics message naming the rejected value.

When harness, model and effort are all omitted, the run uses harness claude, model claude-opus-5-5 and effort medium, exactly as today; omitted Codex model and effort are still resolved from the local Codex configuration.

The CLI accepts --model=<id> and --effort=<level> in addition to --harness=<claude|codex>, in any order, each at most once; any other argument is refused with exit code 4. CLI values override the invocation JSON fields model and effort.
The resolved harness, model and effort stay part of the frozen invocation identity: a restart with a different resolved value is refused as today.

Tests cover catalog lookup for both harnesses (Codex via a scripted model/list response, including pagination and a hidden model), default resolution, CLI flag parsing and precedence, refusal of unknown model and unsupported effort, and a Claude adapter started with a non-Opus catalog model. No test starts a real harness.

README sections 'Start and resume' and 'Quick start' document the selectable models, efforts, the new flags and the unchanged defaults; the statement that Claude is pinned to Opus 5.5 medium is replaced.
npm run typecheck and npm test pass.

tasks.title: Configurable test coverage threshold
criteria: The invocation JSON accepts an optional integer field coverage and the CLI accepts --coverage=<n>; n must be an integer from 1 to 100, otherwise the run is refused with exit code 4. The CLI value overrides the JSON value.
When neither is given, the coverage threshold is 85.
The resolved coverage threshold is part of the frozen invocation identity: a restart with a different resolved threshold is refused like a changed harness, model or effort.
Arguments of project.checks may contain the placeholder {coverage}; the runner replaces it with the resolved threshold, the same way it replaces {change}, {target} and {scope}.
A run whose project.checks contain no argument with {coverage} is refused before allocation with exit code 4 and a diagnostics message saying that a coverage gate check is required.
Every worker prompt states the resolved coverage threshold as a percentage.

Tests cover the default 85, JSON value, CLI override, rejection of 0, 101, 85.5 and non-numeric values, placeholder substitution in a check, refusal without a {coverage} check, and refusal of a restart with a changed threshold.

README documents coverage, --coverage and {coverage}, and its invocation example contains a check that enforces the threshold, for example node --test --experimental-test-coverage --test-coverage-lines={coverage}.
npm run typecheck and npm test pass.

tasks.title: OpenSpec preflight with install offer
criteria: Before any harness check, selection prompt, claim or worktree is created, the runner checks that the OpenSpec CLI is available (openspec --version exits 0) and that openspec/config.yaml exists at origin/<target> of the repository.
The startup is interactive only when both process.stdin and process.stderr are TTYs; all prompts and their explanations are written to stderr so stdout keeps only the existing JSON lines.

Interactive, missing CLI: the runner asks whether to install it with npm install -g @fission-ai/openspec@latest. On yes it runs exactly that command as an argument array, then repeats the check; on no, or when the install or the repeated check fails, it exits with code 4 and diagnostics reason openspec-missing.

Interactive, missing openspec/config.yaml at origin/<target>: the runner asks whether to create the project layout in the working tree (openspec/config.yaml containing 'schema: spec-driven', plus .gitkeep files in the project changes and receipts directories). On yes it creates only the missing files, never commits or pushes, and exits with code 4 and a message to commit and push them; on no it exits with code 4 and diagnostics reason openspec-not-initialized.
Non-interactive: nothing is installed or created and nothing is asked; a missing CLI or config exits with code 4 and the matching diagnostics reason.
When OpenSpec is available and initialized, startup continues without any OpenSpec prompt.
Prompt input, process execution and file creation are injectable so tests script answers and commands; no test runs npm, openspec or a real TTY.
Tests cover: available and initialized; missing CLI with yes and successful install; yes with failing install; no; missing config with yes and with no; and the non-interactive refusals.
README describes the OpenSpec preflight, the install offer and the non-interactive behaviour.
npm run typecheck and npm test pass.

tasks.title: Interactive harness, model, effort and coverage selection
criteria: After the OpenSpec preflight passes, the runner checks the availability of both harnesses with their existing probes: Claude Code 2.1.321 or newer and Codex CLI 0.167.0 or newer; a missing executable counts as unavailable with reason not-installed instead of failing the run.

Interactive (same TTY rule and stderr output as the OpenSpec preflight): the runner shows each harness with its status and version or reason, and asks the user to choose among the available harnesses only; claude is the preselected answer when available. When only one harness is available it is shown and preselected.
After the harness is chosen, the runner lists the models that harness offers (from the OR-1 catalog) and asks for one; claude-opus-5-5 is preselected for Claude, the Codex default model for Codex.
After the model is chosen, the runner lists only the efforts that this harness and model support and asks for one; medium is preselected when supported, otherwise the model's default effort.
Last, the runner asks for the coverage threshold with 85 preselected and accepts only an integer from 1 to 100, asking again on invalid input.
Pressing Enter accepts the preselected answer. A value given by a CLI flag or the invocation JSON is used without asking for it.
When no harness is available, or a harness set by flag or JSON is unavailable, the runner exits with code 4 and a diagnostics message listing each harness and its reason.
Non-interactive: nothing is asked; flags, JSON and defaults (claude, claude-opus-5-5, medium, 85) apply, and the selected harness must be available.

On a restart of an invocation whose state already records a harness, model, effort and coverage, no selection prompt is shown and the recorded selection is reused; a flag or JSON value that differs is refused as today.
The chosen values are used by the run and frozen in its identity exactly like values given by flags.
Prompt input and harness probes are injectable; tests script answers and probe results and never start a real harness.

Tests cover: both harnesses available with default answers; choosing Codex and one of its models and efforts; only one harness available; none available; flag-supplied values skipping their prompts; invalid coverage answer followed by a valid one; non-interactive defaults; restart reusing the recorded selection.
README documents the interactive startup order: OpenSpec, harness availability, harness, model, effort, coverage.
npm run typecheck and npm test pass.

tasks.title: Completion summary with duration and complexity grade
criteria: The runner records the time a task is claimed in its work state; the record survives a restart.

The outcome_report schema gains an optional completion object with summary (string) and grade (one of A, B, C, D, E). The implementation review session must provide it whenever it reports accepted; an accepted report without a valid completion is refused like any other invalid private report.
The review prompt explains the grade: the complexity of the whole task from A (most complex) to E (easiest), and asks for a summary of two or three English sentences describing what the task changed.

When the task is accepted, the controller builds a completion summary of three or four English sentences: the reviewer's summary followed by one sentence stating the wall-clock time from claim to acceptance (formatted like 1h 12m 5s) and the complexity grade.
The accepted event printed to stdout contains summary, durationSeconds and grade, and the final result JSON contains the same data per newly accepted task ID.
Existing receipts stay valid: receipt validation does not require the new data.
Tests cover the duration across a simulated restart, an accepted review without completion being refused, an invalid grade being refused, and the content of the accepted event and the final result.
README documents the completion summary, the A to E scale and where the summary appears.
npm run typecheck and npm test pass.

tasks.title: Graded test planning up to the coverage threshold
criteria: The plan session prompt requires tasks.md to contain a test section in which every planned test has a complexity grade from A (most complex) to E (easiest), listed from E to A.
The planning review prompt requires the reviewer to report changes-required when a planned test lacks a grade or the tests are not listed from E to A.

The work session prompt requires writing tests grade by grade starting with E, calling run_checks after each grade, and continuing to the next harder grade until the coverage gate passes at the resolved threshold; grades left unwritten because the threshold was reached stay unchecked in tasks.md with the note 'not needed: coverage reached'.

The implementation review prompt requires changes-required when the coverage gate did not pass at the resolved threshold or when a harder grade was written while an easier planned grade is still unchecked without that note.
All prompts state the resolved coverage threshold as a percentage.
Tests assert the plan, planning review, work and implementation review prompts contain these instructions and the resolved threshold, using scripted adapters only.
README describes the graded test workflow.
npm run typecheck and npm test pass.

tasks.title: JSONL ledger of all runs for statistics
criteria: Every invocation of the runner, except the hash command, appends exactly one JSON object as one line to $XDG_STATE_HOME/outcome-runner/runs.jsonl (default ~/.local/state/outcome-runner/runs.jsonl) when it ends, whatever its exit code: 0, 3, 4, or a cancellation by SIGINT or SIGTERM.

The file and its directories are created when missing, the file with mode 0600; existing lines are never rewritten or removed, and each record is written with a single append call so records of concurrent runs on one machine do not interleave.

Each record contains: schemaVersion 1, a unique runId, runner package version, hostname, repository top-level path, origin URL, target branch, invocation name, authority reference, startedAt and endedAt as ISO 8601 UTC, durationSeconds, exitCode, status (exhausted, limit-reached, incomplete, cancelled or unavailable) and, for unavailable, the failure reason.

Each record contains the resolved run settings when they were resolved: harness, harness CLI version, model, effort, coverage threshold, maxAccepted, the selected leaves, and whether each setting came from a CLI flag, the invocation JSON, an interactive answer or the default.

Each record contains one entry per task the run worked on or decided about, with: id, change, outcome (accepted, blocked, claimed-elsewhere or not-started), last stage reached, blocking reason when blocked, durationSeconds from claim to acceptance, complexity grade and completion summary when accepted, number of worker sessions per purpose, number of planning and implementation review rounds, number of findings per review round, final check commands with their outcomes, and the PR number and URL when one exists.
Each record contains token usage per task and per run when the harness reports it, and null otherwise.
Records never contain the authority instruction text, worker prompts, private worker output, check output, file contents or environment variables.
A failure to write the ledger is reported on stderr and does not change the runner's exit code or result.
README documents the ledger path, that one line is written per run, and every field of the record with its type.

Tests use a temporary XDG_STATE_HOME and cover: records for exit codes 0, 3 and 4 and for cancellation; two runs appending two parseable lines; required fields and per-task data for an accepted and a blocked task; absence of the authority instruction, prompts and private output; and an unwritable ledger leaving the exit code unchanged. No test starts a real harness.
npm run typecheck and npm test pass.

tasks.title: Harness-analysed test framework preflight
criteria: After the OpenSpec preflight and the harness, model, effort and coverage selection, and before any claim is made, the runner analyses the repository at origin/<target> with the selected harness, model and effort in one read-only session.

The analysis session runs in a temporary detached worktree of origin/<target> created outside the repository and removed afterwards, even when the analysis fails. It uses the existing broker with read-only access to every tracked file, has no write access, no run_checks and no shell, and reports through a private structured tool.

The analysis report lists every detected technology (language, runtime, framework or build tool) with the repository paths that prove it; for each technology, the test frameworks already present and whether they enforce line, branch and function coverage thresholds; and, for each technology without a prepared test framework, one to three recommended test frameworks, each with a one-sentence rationale, the install commands as command and argument arrays, and the exact file changes that run the tests with line, branch and function coverage thresholds equal to the resolved coverage threshold (85 by default). The runner refuses a report that misses any of these parts.

A technology is prepared when the analysis finds a test framework for it that enforces the resolved coverage threshold. When every technology is prepared, startup continues without any test framework prompt.

Interactive (same TTY rule and stderr output as the OpenSpec preflight): the runner prints the detected technologies with their evidence and existing frameworks, then, for each technology that is not prepared, asks the user to choose one of the recommended frameworks (the first is preselected) or to skip it.

Before running anything, the runner shows the exact install commands and file changes of the chosen recommendation and asks for confirmation. Only after a yes does it run the install commands as argument arrays, never through a shell, in the working tree, and apply the file changes. File changes must stay inside the repository, outside .git, the queue, the receipts and the OpenSpec changes directories; otherwise the recommendation is refused.

The runner never commits or pushes these changes; after a successful setup it exits with code 4 and a message listing the changed files to commit and push. When the user skips or declines a technology, or an install command fails, it exits with code 4 and diagnostics reason test-framework-missing naming the technologies left unprepared.

Non-interactive: the analysis still runs, but nothing is installed or changed and nothing is asked; when any technology is not prepared, the runner exits with code 4 and diagnostics reason test-framework-missing with the analysis report.
When the analysis session fails or returns an invalid report, the runner exits with code 4 and diagnostics reason test-framework-analysis-failed; no claim is made.

The harness session, prompt input, command execution and file writes are injectable; tests use scripted adapters and answers, and no test starts a real harness, runs a package manager or uses a real TTY.

Tests cover: all technologies prepared; one unprepared technology with the first recommendation accepted; choosing a later recommendation; skip; declined confirmation; failing install command; a file change outside the allowed paths refused; a non-default coverage threshold passed to the analysis; a repository with two technologies; non-interactive refusal; analysis failure and invalid report; and removal of the temporary worktree in every case.
README documents the harness-based technology analysis, how recommendations are chosen and confirmed, the coverage thresholds they apply and the non-interactive behaviour.
npm run typecheck and npm test pass.

tasks.title: Automatic semantic versioning from Conventional Commits
criteria: Add scripts/release.ts, TypeScript with erasable syntax only and Node built-ins only, that computes the next Semantic Versioning 2.0.0 version from the Conventional Commits 1.0.0 messages (subject and body) of every commit reachable from HEAD and not from the latest tag matching vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, including commits of merged branches.

Bump rules: a type followed by '!' before the colon, or a 'BREAKING CHANGE:' or 'BREAKING-CHANGE:' footer, bumps MAJOR and resets MINOR and PATCH; otherwise any feat bumps MINOR and resets PATCH; otherwise any fix or perf bumps PATCH; otherwise there is no release. Scopes in the type, such as feat(work-queue), are accepted. Merge commit subjects and messages that do not follow Conventional Commits are ignored.
Commits whose subject starts with 'chore(release):' are ignored, so a release commit never causes another release.
When no vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH tag exists, the first release tags the current package.json version without bumping it.

On a release the script sets the version in package.json and in package-lock.json (its root version and packages[""].version), leaving every other byte of both files unchanged; prepends to CHANGELOG.md, creating it when missing, a section '## X.Y.Z - YYYY-MM-DD' with the groups 'Breaking changes', 'Features' and 'Fixes', each listing the commit descriptions without the type prefix and with the short hash, and omitting empty groups; creates the commit 'chore(release): vX.Y.Z' containing only these files; and creates the annotated tag vX.Y.Z on it. The script never pushes.
With --dry-run the script prints the next version, or 'no release', and the changelog section, and changes no file, commit or tag.

Add .github/workflows/release.yml: on push to main, with concurrency group release and cancel-in-progress false, permissions contents write, checkout with full history and tags, Node 24, npm ci, npm run typecheck and npm test; then it runs the release script and, when a release was made, pushes the commit and the tag in one atomic push without force and creates a GitHub Release for the tag whose notes are the new changelog section. When main moved meanwhile and the push is rejected, the job fails without retrying or force-pushing.
The workflow does not release when the pushed head commit is a release commit.

package.json gains the script release:dry-run running node scripts/release.ts --dry-run; the test script also runs scripts/*.test.ts and keeps the 85% line, branch and function coverage thresholds; tsconfig.json includes scripts so npm run typecheck checks it. The build output in dist does not include scripts.

scripts/release.test.ts runs against temporary Git repositories and covers: breaking change by '!' and by footer, feat, fix, perf, no release, scoped types, merge commits, ignored release commits, the bootstrap release without tags, package.json and package-lock.json changes limited to the version, the CHANGELOG section and its empty groups omitted, the annotated tag, and a dry run that changes nothing.
docs/releasing.md documents the bump rules, the commit message format with examples, the workflow, the dry run and what to do when a release push is rejected.
npm run typecheck and npm test pass.

tasks.title: Animated mascot module
criteria: Add mascot/mascot.ts, TypeScript with erasable syntax only and Node built-ins only, with an original small mascot drawn with Unicode block characters and ANSI colours, at most 7 lines high and 20 columns wide. It is inspired by the style of a compact terminal logo but does not reproduce the Claude Code logo or any other existing logo or character.

The module offers exactly these moods, each with its own eyes, mouth and colour: happy (green), angry (red), celebrating (yellow, with sparkles), content (cyan), sleepy (blue), sad (blue), startled (yellow) and dizzy (magenta).

It exports one function that plays a given mood with a given caption line: an animation of 3 to 6 frames lasting at most 1.5 seconds in total, redrawn in place, after which the last frame stays on screen followed by the caption. The returned promise resolves when the animation ends and never rejects.

It writes to stderr by default and writes nothing when the stream is not a TTY or the environment variable OUTCOME_RUNNER_MASCOT is 0. With NO_COLOR set it keeps the same shapes without colours. With TERM=dumb it prints only the last frame and the caption, without cursor movement.
The cursor is hidden while an animation plays and always shown again afterwards, also when the animation is stopped through an AbortSignal option or a write fails.
The output stream, TTY detection, environment, frame timer and abort signal are injectable.

mascot/mascot.test.ts uses a fake timer and an in-memory stream, never sleeps, and covers: every mood with its frame count, height and width limits and the 1.5-second limit; the caption after the last frame; no output for a non-TTY stream and for OUTCOME_RUNNER_MASCOT=0; no colour codes with NO_COLOR; only the last frame with TERM=dumb; the cursor restored after an abort and after a failing write; and a promise that never rejects.
package.json: the test script also runs mascot/*.test.ts and keeps the 85% line, branch and function coverage thresholds. tsconfig.json includes mascot so npm run typecheck checks it.
mascot/README.md shows the last frame of every mood as a plain-text preview and documents the exported function and its options.
npm run typecheck and npm test pass.

tasks.title: Show the mascot when tasks and runs end
criteria: The runner plays the mascot from mascot/mascot.ts when a task or a run ends: happy when a task is accepted and merged; angry when a task is blocked; celebrating when a run ends exhausted; content when a run ends limit-reached; sleepy when a run ends incomplete without blockers, only waiting for claimed or dependent work; sad when a run ends incomplete with blockers; startled when a run is cancelled by SIGINT or SIGTERM; dizzy when the runner exits with code 4.
Every event status the runner reports and every final run status maps to exactly one mood; a test fails when a status the runner can produce has no mood.
Captions: for a task, the task ID and what happened (for example 'OR-1 merged' or 'OR-1 blocked: <reason, at most 60 characters>'); for a run, its status and the accepted and remaining counts.
The mascot is written to stderr only; the JSON lines on stdout are byte-for-byte unchanged.
The flag --no-mascot turns the mascot off and is accepted together with the other CLI flags; OUTCOME_RUNNER_MASCOT=0 also turns it off.
A SIGINT or SIGTERM during an animation stops it through its abort signal, so the cursor is shown again before the runner finishes cancelling.
A mascot failure never changes the runner result, its exit code or its state.

Tests use an injected mascot player and cover: the mood and caption for every task event and run status, including exit code 4 and a blocked reason longer than 60 characters; --no-mascot and OUTCOME_RUNNER_MASCOT=0; stdout identical with and without the mascot; abort on SIGINT during an animation; and a failing player leaving the result and exit code unchanged.
README documents when each mood appears, links mascot/README.md for the previews, and explains how to turn the mascot off.
npm run typecheck and npm test pass.

tasks.title: Install test prerequisites in the release workflow
criteria: The test suite runs openspec validate through the runner's planning check, so npm test fails in GitHub Actions when the OpenSpec CLI is missing; the first Release run on main failed this way with 27 failing tests.

Before npm test, .github/workflows/release.yml installs the OpenSpec CLI with npm install -g @fission-ai/openspec@1.17.0 and prints openspec --version in a separate step, so a missing or broken CLI fails before the tests.
No other step of the workflow changes: triggers, concurrency, permissions, checkout, Node 24, npm ci, typecheck, test, release script, atomic push and GitHub Release stay as they are.
docs/releasing.md lists the OpenSpec CLI and its pinned version as a prerequisite of the workflow's test step and explains that the version is updated in the workflow file.
npm run typecheck and npm test pass.

tasks.title: Tolerate a stale pull request head after a push
criteria: Defect: when the target advanced while a task waited in the merge stage, the runner integrated the target, pushed a new head and then read the pull request at once; GitHub still reported the previous head, so the task was blocked with 'Checked head or target changed' although nothing foreign had changed (OR-2, PR #14, 2026-11-10). A restart with the same invocation then merged it.

In the merge stage, when the pull request reports a headRefOid different from the recorded tested head but origin's branch ref (read with git ls-remote origin refs/heads/<branch>) equals the recorded head, the runner reads the pull request again with the same poll interval and view limit as the existing mergeability wait (3 seconds, 100 views by default) until the reported head equals the recorded head, and then merges.

GitHubHost.merge applies the same rule: its settled merge view also keeps polling while the reported headRefOid lags behind the expected head and origin's branch ref equals the expected head, instead of failing at once.

When origin's branch ref differs from the recorded head, or the pull request still reports another head after the view limit, the task is blocked with 'Checked head or target changed' as today and nothing is merged. The local HEAD check and the merge with --match-head-commit <recorded head> stay as they are.
The wait re-runs no checks and creates no commit, push or pull request.

Tests use scripted hosts and Git fixtures and cover: a pull request reporting the previous head for several views and then the recorded head is merged without blocking; the full race of a target advance during the merge stage followed by a stale head; origin's branch moved by someone else blocks without merging; a head still stale after the view limit blocks without merging; and the same cases inside GitHubHost.merge. No test waits in real time.
npm run typecheck and npm test pass.

tasks.title: Update documentation and archive the OpenSpec change before merge
criteria: The stage order of a task becomes: implementation review accepted, documentation, documentation review, project checks, archive, receipt, publish, pull request, merge. Every new stage is saved in the run state and resumes after a restart without repeating a completed step; in particular the archive never runs twice.

Documentation stage: a worker session with the selected harness updates every documentation file inside the task scopes (README files, Markdown files and directories such as docs) so that it matches the implemented behaviour and the task criteria. It may write only documentation files inside the task scopes. Documentation outside the scopes that needs changes is reported as findings and listed in the pull request body under 'Documentation outside scope'.

Documentation review stage: an independent review session checks the documentation changes against the implementation, the criteria and the scope, and reports accepted only with zero findings. Like the planning and implementation stages it allows at most 4 rounds; when unresolved the task is blocked with 'Documentation review remains unresolved'. After acceptance the project checks run again and must pass.

Archive stage: the runner archives the OpenSpec change with the new optional project command archive, run as an argument array in the worktree with the {change} placeholder; the default is openspec archive {change} --yes. The archive moves the change directory to <changes>/archive/<YYYY-MM-DD>-<change> and applies the spec deltas to openspec/specs. A failing archive command blocks the task with its bounded failure output.

After the archive, the specification binding follows the files: each bound path is re-keyed to its archived path, and the runner verifies that every bound file exists there with the same hash; otherwise the task is blocked with 'Archived specification differs from binding'. Later integrity checks use the archived paths.

The result manifest accepts paths inside the task scopes, the archived change directory and the openspec/specs files written by the archive; any other path still blocks the task. The receipt records the archived specification paths, and receipt validation accepts them. Existing receipts that reference unarchived paths stay valid.
When the target advances, a change of the target to the same openspec/specs files or to the archived change directory blocks the task like a change inside its scope.
The pull request body lists the updated documentation files and the archived change directory.

Tests use scripted adapters, Git fixtures and a scripted archive command and cover: documentation written only inside the scopes; documentation outside the scopes reported in the pull request body; a documentation review that needs a second round; an unresolved documentation review; checks re-run after documentation; the archive relocation and spec update; re-keyed binding and a hash mismatch after archive; manifest acceptance of archived and spec paths and rejection of other paths; receipt validation with archived paths and with an existing unarchived receipt; a restart between archive and receipt not archiving again; and a target change to the same spec file blocking the task.
README documents the new stages, the archive command and its default, and where archived changes and updated specs end up.
npm run typecheck and npm test pass.

tasks.title: Pixel mascot redesign approved by the owner
criteria: Replace the OR-10 mascot art in mascot/mascot.ts with the pixel sprite the owner approved on 2026-11-11, derived from the owner's reference image: antennae, a wide body with two eye slots and X-shaped legs. The exported function, its options and the eight moods do not change.

The sprite is 11 by 8 pixels. Rows 0 to 5, top to bottom, are '...B...B...', '....B.B....', '..BBBBBBB..', '.BBBBBBBBB.', 'BB00BBB11BB', 'BB00BBB11BB'. Rows 6 and 7 are the legs in one of two poses: pose 0 '..B.BBB.B..' and '.B.B...B.B.'; pose 1 '..B.BBB.B..' and 'B.B.....B.B'. '.' is empty, B is body, 0 is the left eye and 1 the right eye.

Each eye is 2 by 2 pixels at columns 2 and 3 (left) and 8 and 7 (right, mirrored) of rows 4 and 5. Eye patterns, top row then bottom row: open 'WW','WK'; happy 'WW','BB'; angry 'BW','WK'; sad 'WW','KW'; sleepy 'BB','WW'; wide 'WW','WW'; swirlA 'KW','WK'; swirlB 'WK','KW'; star 'SW','WS'. W is eye white (colour 231), K pupil (16), S sparkle (226). Cheeks C (211) sit at row 5, columns 1 and 9. A tear T (117) sits at column 3 of row 6 or 7.

Rendering uses two pixel rows per text line, so the sprite is 11 columns by 4 lines: a cell with both pixels set prints '▀' with the top pixel as foreground and the bottom pixel as background ANSI 256 colour, a cell with only the top or only the bottom pixel prints '▀' or '▄' in that colour, and an empty cell prints a space. With NO_COLOR no colour codes are written, eye whites and tears print as empty, and every other pixel prints as solid.

Body colours: happy 78, angry 160, celebrating 220, content 44, sleepy 69, sad 61, startled 208, dizzy 170. Decorations print one space to the right of the sprite on a given line: '♪' (229), '#' (196), '+', '*' and '.' sparkles (229, 213, 117), 'z' and 'zZ' (153), '!' and '!!' (196). Every frame, decorations and offsets included, is at most 4 lines high and 14 columns wide.

Frames per mood, in order (eyes, legs pose, extras): happy: open/0; happy/1; happy/0 with cheeks; happy/1 with cheeks and '♪' on line 0. angry: angry eyes, legs 0, offset 0, 1, 0, 1 columns to the right, then offset 0 with '#' on line 0. celebrating: star eyes, legs 0, 1, 0, 1, with sparkles changing between lines 0 to 3 each frame. content: open/0; sleepy/0; open/1. sleepy: sleepy eyes with 'z' on line 1, then 'z' on line 0, then 'zZ' on line 0. sad: sad eyes with the tear at row 6, row 7, no tear with legs 1, then the tear at row 7. startled: open/1; wide/0 with '!'; wide/1 with '!!'. dizzy: swirlA with '*' on line 0; swirlB offset 1 with '*' on line 1; swirlA with '*' on line 2; swirlB offset 1 with '*' on line 0.

The OR-10 rules still hold: 3 to 6 frames and at most 1.5 seconds per mood, redrawn in place, last frame left on screen with the caption, stderr only, TTY only, OUTCOME_RUNNER_MASCOT=0, TERM=dumb printing only the last frame, cursor hidden while playing and restored after an abort or a failed write, and a promise that never rejects.

mascot/mascot.test.ts checks: the sprite rows and leg poses; every eye pattern and its mirror; the frame sequence of every mood; the half-block rendering for top-only, bottom-only, both and empty cells with the right foreground and background colours; the NO_COLOR rendering; at most 4 lines and 14 columns for every frame; and the unchanged OR-10 rules.
mascot/README.md replaces the previews with the NO_COLOR last frame of every mood and states that the design comes from the owner's reference sprite.
npm run typecheck and npm test pass.

tasks.title: Many runners per branch, each in its own worktree
criteria: The run target is the branch checked out where the runner starts. When the invocation omits project.target and authority.target, both resolve to that branch; when either is given and differs from it, the run is refused with exit code 4 and diagnostics reason target-differs-from-current-branch. A detached HEAD is refused with reason detached-head, and a branch missing on origin with reason target-missing-on-origin. The resolved target is part of the frozen invocation identity and is recorded in every receipt.

Every task is still worked in its own worktree outside the checkout and reaches the target only through a pull request into that branch, merged by the runner. The runner never changes the working tree, index or local branch of the checkout it was started from.

Several invocations may run at the same time in one clone and on one branch. The per-clone exclusive lock and the per-clone ownership file are replaced by a per-invocation lock and per-invocation ownership: a second process of the same invocation is still refused at once, and a different invocation never inherits or overrides another invocation's unfinished work.

Git operations on the shared repository (fetch, worktree add and remove, branch creation and deletion, claims ledger commits and pushes) are serialized between runners of the same clone with a lock held only for one group of Git operations. A runner waits up to 60 seconds for it; the lock is released when its holder exits or crashes. Concurrent runners never fail because of Git index or ref lock files.

Runners of the same clone share tasks through the existing claims ledger, each invocation with its own claimant: two runners never work on the same task or on tasks with overlapping scopes at the same time.

After a task's pull request is merged and its acceptance is confirmed, the runner removes the task worktree, deletes the local task branch and deletes the remote task branch. A cleanup failure is reported in the accepted event and does not change the result. Worktrees and branches of blocked or unfinished tasks are kept so the task can resume.
On start, the runner removes leftover worktrees and local branches of tasks its invocation already has accepted.

Tests use scripted adapters and Git fixtures and cover: two invocations running concurrently in one clone completing different tasks and merging into the start branch; a second process of the same invocation refused; a run started from a feature branch opening its pull requests against that branch; target mismatch, detached HEAD and missing remote branch refused; concurrent fetch and worktree operations not failing on Git lock files; worktree, local and remote branch removed after merge; a cleanup failure reported without changing the result; leftovers removed on start; and a blocked task keeping its worktree.
README replaces 'Give each machine its own clone' with how to run many runners on one branch, explains that the target is the branch the runner starts from, and describes worktree cleanup.
npm run typecheck and npm test pass.

tasks.title: Log every logical step before it starts
criteria: Before the runner starts each logical step it writes one clear, short line to stderr, so a person watching the console always sees what the runner is about to do. The line is written before the step has any effect.

Logical steps include at least: start of the run with invocation, harness, model and effort; each preflight (harness version, OpenSpec, test framework); claiming a task; preparing its worktree; each setup command; the planning session; the planning check; the implementation session; each product check; commit and push; creating or updating the pull request; waiting for mergeability and checks; integrating an advanced target; merging; recording the receipt and acceptance; worktree and branch cleanup; and the end of the run with its outcome.

Each line has the form '[outcome-runner] HH:MM:SS <task id or run> <step>: <message>', is a single line of at most 120 characters, in English, and never contains secrets, worker output, file contents or private diagnostics.
Waits and polling loops (mergeability, stale pull request head, Git lock) log once when the wait starts, not on every poll. A step that is retried logs again with the attempt number.
On resume, steps already completed in the durable state are not logged as started again; a step continued from state logs with 'resuming'.
stdout, exit codes, the diagnostics file and receipts are unchanged. Step lines go through an injected output so tests can capture them.

Tests use scripted adapters and Git fixtures and cover: the ordered step lines of a task accepted end to end, each appearing before the effect of its step; a blocked task whose last line names the step where it was blocked; a polling wait logged once; a retried step logged with its attempt; a resumed run not repeating completed steps; the line format and 120-character limit; and stdout identical to a run without step logging.
README describes the step lines on stderr and their format.
npm run typecheck and npm test pass.

tasks.title: Refuse incomplete task sets and explain every unfinished result
criteria: Before claiming anything, the runner checks that every dependency of every task it will work (leaves, or all authority tasks) is either in that set or already accepted. Otherwise the run is refused with exit code 4 and diagnostics reason dependencies-outside-invocation, listing each task and its missing dependencies. The runner never again exits 3 because a dependency outside the invocation can never be worked.

An incomplete result (exit code 3) always names, for every remaining task, why it was not finished: blocked with its reason and stage, waiting for a named dependency, waiting for a named foreign claim with overlapping scopes, or stopped by maxAccepted. blockers is never empty while remaining is not.
state.json carries the invocation status the runner last reached (running, incomplete, blocked, completed, released) instead of staying at starting, and is updated before the process exits.

Tests use scripted adapters and Git fixtures and cover: leaves missing a dependency refused with the missing tasks named; a dependency already accepted allowed; each kind of unfinished reason in the incomplete result; and the final status written to state for a completed, an incomplete and a blocked run.
README describes the dependency check, the unfinished reasons and the state status.
npm run typecheck and npm test pass.

tasks.title: Dispose of an invocation with one command
criteria: outcome-runner dispose <invocation file> ends an invocation the owner no longer wants: it releases the invocation's ownership, removes its claims of unaccepted tasks from the claims ledger with one commit naming the invocation, and marks its state released. Accepted tasks, receipts and merged pull requests are not touched.

Dispose is refused with exit code 4 and a clear reason while a process of that invocation is running, and when the file does not match a known invocation state. Running it twice is safe and reports that nothing was left to release.

By default the worktrees and local and remote branches of its unaccepted tasks are kept and listed, so finished work can still be inspected; with --remove-work they are removed. Open pull requests of the invocation are listed and never merged.
Disposing never touches the ownership, claims or state of another invocation or another repository.
Dispose prints a JSON summary on stdout with the released claims, kept or removed worktrees and branches, and open pull requests.

Tests use Git fixtures and cover: claims released and ownership freed so a new invocation can start; accepted work untouched; a running invocation refused; repeated dispose; work kept by default and removed with --remove-work; and another invocation left untouched.
README describes when and how to dispose of an invocation, replacing any manual editing of ownership files or the claims branch.
npm run typecheck and npm test pass.

tasks.title: Recover when the target advances into a task scope
criteria: When the target branch has changed files inside a task's scopes since the task's base, the runner no longer blocks the task with Target changed outcome scope. It merges the new target into the task branch in the task worktree and records the new base in durable state.

A merge without conflicts is followed again by the product checks, the implementation review and the documentation review before the pull request is published or updated. A previous acceptance of those steps is never reused for the new base.

A merge with conflicts gives the worker one implementation session to resolve them inside the task scopes, followed by the same checks and reviews. The task is blocked with reason target-conflict-unresolved and the conflicting paths only when that session fails or the reviews do not accept the result.
The same recovery applies whether the target advanced before publish, while waiting for checks, or before merge, and survives a restart of the invocation.

Tests use scripted adapters and Git fixtures and cover: a clean merge of an advanced target re-running checks and reviews before merge; a conflict resolved by the worker; an unresolved conflict blocking with its paths; recovery resumed after a restart; and a target change outside the scopes still integrated as before.
README describes what happens when the target advances during a run.
npm run typecheck and npm test pass.

tasks.title: Keep invocation work across runner upgrades and added tasks
criteria: The frozen invocation identity covers what the owner authorised (authority, target, tasks and their hashes, harness, model, effort, coverage, checks), not defaults or settings introduced by a newer runner. Upgrading the runner never by itself makes an unfinished invocation unrecoverable.

When a newer runner requires a setting the invocation lacks, the run is refused with exit code 4 and a reason naming the missing setting and an example. Adding exactly that setting to the invocation file keeps the durable state and resumes the unfinished work; the change is recorded in state and in later receipts.

The owner may add tasks to authority.tasks of an unfinished invocation. Existing claims, worktrees, reviews and accepted tasks are kept, the new tasks are worked after them in queue order, and the addition is recorded in state. Removing or changing a task hash is still refused as before.

Tests cover: an unfinished invocation resumed by a newer runner with unchanged settings; a missing required setting reported and then accepted without losing state; added tasks worked while existing work resumes; and a changed task hash still refused.
README describes upgrading the runner during an unfinished invocation and adding tasks to it.
npm run typecheck and npm test pass.

tasks.title: Durable review round budgets
criteria: Planning, implementation and documentation review rounds are counted per task in durable state, so a restart continues the same count instead of granting new rounds silently.

A failing planning check or product check gives the worker its own bounded number of fix attempts and does not use up review rounds; the blocked reason says whether reviews or checks ran out and how many rounds of each were used.
A blocked task gets a fresh budget only when the owner restarts with --retry <task id>; the retry is recorded in state and in the receipt.

Tests use scripted adapters and cover: counts kept across a restart; check failures not consuming review rounds; the blocked reason naming the exhausted budget; and --retry granting one new budget that is recorded.
README describes the review and check budgets and --retry.
npm run typecheck and npm test pass.

tasks.title: No temporary diagnostic files in published work
criteria: The worker prompt tells the worker to delete every scratch or diagnostic file it created before finishing, using delete_file.
The implementation review is asked to reject files that only served diagnosis, such as temporary debug tests, and to name them in its findings.
test/zz-debug-capture.test.ts and any other leftover diagnostic file on the target are removed when no test or product code depends on them.
Tests use scripted adapters and cover the worker and review prompts mentioning leftover files, and a review that names a leftover file sending the task back to the worker.
npm run typecheck and npm test pass.

tasks.title: Clear CLI usage, version and install guidance
criteria: outcome-runner --version prints the installed version and --help prints the commands and their arguments, both with exit code 0.

outcome-runner hash accepts a queue file and optional task ids and prints only those hashes. A missing file or an unknown task id is reported in one line on stderr naming the argument, with exit code 4, and never as a raw stack trace.
Every run and diagnostics file includes the runner version, so an outdated global install is visible.

README gives the exact global install and update command, including --allow-scripts=outcome-runner, and says to update the global runner only while no invocation is unfinished or after checking that it can resume.
Tests cover --version, --help, hash with task ids, a missing queue file and an unknown task id.
npm run typecheck and npm test pass.

tasks.title: Release workflow survives merges close together
criteria: Release runs triggered by pushes to main never run at the same time; a queued run starts after the previous one finishes.

When the release push is rejected because main advanced, the workflow fetches, recomputes the version from the new main and retries a bounded number of times, without creating a duplicate tag or changelog entry.

Tests of the workflow definition and the release scripts with Git fixtures show that two pull requests merged within a few minutes produce two consecutive releases or one release containing both, and no failed push. All criteria are verified locally with these tests; observing hosted GitHub Actions runs is not required and is not part of the evidence.
The release scripts have tests for recomputing after main advanced and for not duplicating an existing tag; npm test passes.
docs describe the release behaviour for close merges.

tasks.title: Secret scanning without false positives on test fixtures
criteria: A .gitguardian.yaml in the repository root has exactly this shape: version: 2, and secret.ignored_matches with a single entry whose name describes the /etc/passwd test fixture and whose match is the literal string /etc/passwd. It has no paths-ignore or other exclusions, so all product and test code stays scanned.

A test in scripts reads .gitguardian.yaml and checks the shape above: version 2, exactly one ignored_matches entry with match /etc/passwd, and no paths-ignore or other exclusion. The shape given here is the whole contract; no external documentation, hosted GitGuardian scanner or network access is needed or part of the evidence.
docs explain how to add a reviewed false positive to the configuration instead of marking it by hand in the dashboard.

tasks.title: Merge the advanced target in the worktree and merge only while origin is unchanged
criteria: Owners may merge pull requests into the target while invocations run, including changes inside a running task's scopes. A task is never blocked only because the target advanced; the reason Target changed outcome scope is no longer produced.

Before publishing and again before merging, the runner fetches origin/<target>. When it differs from the commit the task branch was last integrated with, the runner merges origin/<target> into the task branch inside the task worktree, never in the checkout it was started from, and runs the frozen product checks on the merged result. When the merge brought changes inside the task scopes, the implementation review runs again on the merged result.

Immediately before merging the pull request, the runner fetches origin/<target> again and compares it with the target commit it merged and checked. Only when they are equal does it merge, and it merges with the exact checked pull request head (for example gh pr merge --match-head-commit), so no unchecked combination reaches the target.

When origin/<target> advanced again in the meantime, the runner repeats the worktree merge, checks and comparison. After 5 consecutive attempts without an unchanged target the task is blocked with reason target-keeps-advancing, keeping its worktree and branch so a restart continues.

A worktree merge with conflicts gives the worker one implementation session to resolve them inside the task scopes, followed by checks and review; otherwise the task is blocked with reason target-conflict-unresolved naming the conflicting paths. The durable state records each integrated target commit, so a restart resumes from the last one.
Each worktree merge, comparison with origin and retry is logged as a step line, with the attempt number when retried.

Tests use scripted adapters and Git fixtures and cover: a target advanced inside the task scopes merged in the worktree, checked, reviewed and accepted; a target advanced outside the scopes merged and checked without a new review; origin advancing between the check and the merge causing a repeat; the attempt limit blocking with target-keeps-advancing; a changed pull request head refusing the merge; a conflict resolved and an unresolved conflict blocking with its paths; a restart resuming from the recorded target commit; and the start checkout left untouched.
README replaces the advice not to merge into the target during a run with how the runner integrates an advanced target.
npm run typecheck and npm test pass.

tasks.title: Send a rejected integration back to the worker before blocking
criteria: When the checks, the implementation review or the documentation review of an integrated result without conflicts do not accept it, the runner gives the worker one implementation session with the failed check output or the review findings, inside the task scopes, instead of blocking the task at once with target-integration-rejected.

After that session the runner runs the frozen product checks, the implementation review and the documentation review on the result again. Only when they accept does the task continue to publishing and merging; otherwise it is blocked with reason target-integration-rejected, recording the last findings or check output.

The send-back session and the reviews after it are recorded in the integration entry of the durable state before each next effect, so a restart resumes at the recorded step and never grants a second send-back session for the same integrated target commit.
The send-back session and its outcome are logged as step lines.

Tests use scripted adapters and Git fixtures and cover: a documentation review rejection fixed by the send-back session and accepted; an implementation review rejection fixed and accepted; a failed check fixed and accepted; a send-back session whose result is still rejected blocking with target-integration-rejected and its findings; and a restart after the send-back session resuming without a second session.
README describes the send-back session in the integration section and the target-integration-rejected reason.
npm run typecheck and npm test pass.

tasks.title: Wait for claimed and dependent tasks instead of ending the run
criteria: When no remaining task can be picked and every blocker of every remaining task is waiting-for-claim or waiting-for-dependency, the runner does not end with incomplete: it waits a poll interval, pulls the claims ledger and the target again, recomputes done tasks, and picks the next free task.

The poll interval defaults to 60 seconds and may be set by the invocation field pollSeconds, an integer from 5 through 3600; an invalid value is refused at startup with exit code 4 and diagnostics naming it.

The run still ends with incomplete and the existing blockers when a remaining task is blocked in this invocation's own state or depends on such a task, so a run never waits for work nobody can finish; it ends with exhausted or limit-reached exactly as before when those apply.

While waiting the runner logs one step line per poll naming the tasks it waits for and the hosts holding them, and a cancel signal during the wait ends the run with cancelled without a further effect.

Tests use scripted adapters, a fake clock and Git fixtures and cover: a task claimed elsewhere that becomes done and lets the run pick the next task; a dependency merged by another runner that becomes free; a claim released by dispose that becomes free; a self-blocked task ending incomplete without waiting; a cancel during the wait; and an invalid pollSeconds refused.
README describes waiting for free work, pollSeconds and when a run still ends incomplete.
npm run typecheck and npm test pass.

tasks.title: Claim leases so a stale or blocked claim does not freeze its scopes
criteria: A runner that holds a claim renews it in the claims ledger at least every leaseSeconds / 3 while it works the task; leaseSeconds defaults to 1800 and may be set in the invocation as an integer from 300 through 86400, invalid values refused at startup with exit code 4.

A claim whose last renewal is older than its lease is stale: other runners ignore it when choosing free work and when explaining blockers, and a runner may claim that task with a ledger update that only succeeds if the stale claim is still the current one, so two runners never both win a takeover.

When a task is blocked, the runner that holds its claim releases the claim in the ledger before continuing, keeping the blocked work and its branch for inspection, so the scopes of a blocked task stop excluding other tasks on every host.
A runner whose claim was taken over notices it before its next effect on the target or the pull request, stops that task without pushing or merging, and records reason claim-lost.
Claims written by earlier runner versions without renewal data are treated as renewed at claimedAt.

Tests use scripted adapters, a fake clock and Git fixtures and cover: renewal during long work; takeover of a stale claim by exactly one of two competing runners; release of a blocked task's claim letting another runner pick an overlapping task; claim-lost stopping the previous holder before merge; and a legacy claim without renewal data.
README describes claim leases, renewal, takeover, release on block, claim-lost and leaseSeconds.
npm run typecheck and npm test pass.

tasks.title: Merge retries that tolerate pending checks, a behind pull request and release commits
criteria: When the settled pull request is OPEN with the checked head but mergeStateStatus is BEHIND, the runner treats it as an advanced target and returns to the catch-up and publish steps instead of blocking with operation-incomplete.

When mergeStateStatus is BLOCKED, UNSTABLE or UNKNOWN while required checks are still pending, the runner keeps polling the pull request for up to 30 minutes before blocking with reason merge-not-eligible and the last status; a failed required check blocks at once with merge-not-eligible and the check names.

A target advance whose changed paths are only package.json version fields, package-lock.json version fields and CHANGELOG.md from a release commit does not count toward the target attempt limit, and the limit of target attempts is raised from 5 to 10.
Each retry and its reason are recorded in durable state before the next effect and logged as step lines, so a restart resumes at the recorded attempt count.

Tests use scripted adapters and Git fixtures and cover: BEHIND leading to catch-up and a merge; pending checks that turn green and merge; a failed required check blocking with merge-not-eligible; a release-only advance not consuming an attempt; and the attempt limit reached with target-keeps-advancing.
README describes merge eligibility retries, merge-not-eligible and the release-commit exception to the attempt limit.
npm run typecheck and npm test pass.
